hook.text: A mean and a variance sum up one random variable. But the random variables you'll meet keep taking the same few shapes... and those shapes have names.

bernoulli.text: Start with the smallest. One visitor either signs up or doesn't, with a chance of, say, point three. One yes or no is a Bernoulli trial.

binomial.text: Now show the page to two hundred visitors, who each sign up with a chance of three in a hundred, and count the yeses.

six.text: That count is binomial. Six is the likeliest number, and the chances fall away on either side.

ten.text: Ten or more? That happens about eight percent of the time.

alone.text: But it only holds if every visitor decides alone, with the same chance. A crowd sent by one TV ad, all behaving alike, makes the count swing far wider.

poisson-in.text: And some counts have no fixed number of tries at all. Just a rate.

poisson.text: Say a help desk gets three tickets an hour, on average, each arriving on its own. The count in any one hour is Poisson.

spike.text: So how often does an hour bring eight or more, a spike worth staffing for? About one hour in eighty-four.

simulate.text: Simulate a hundred thousand hours to check, and spikes come up one point one seven percent of the time. Close to the formula's one point one nine.

same.text: A Poisson's mean and variance are the same number, here three. So if real counts vary far more than their average, events are clumping... and the Poisson will understate the spikes.

geometric-in.text: One more kind of count is worth a name.

geometric.text: Count the tries until the first success. If each sales call closes one time in five, the calls until the first sale are geometric.

five.text: On average, that's five calls. But the likeliest number is one... and eleven percent of the time, it takes more than ten.

choose.text: So picking a model comes down to what you're counting.

leaves.text: One yes or no is Bernoulli. Successes in a fixed number of tries, binomial. Tries until the first success, geometric. Events at a steady rate, with no fixed number, Poisson.

whole.text: All four count in whole numbers. If two point seven makes sense, you're measuring, not counting.

exact.text: Measurements work differently. Take waiting times, which are often exponential: short waits are common, and long ones rare.

five-min.text: Say they average five minutes. What's the chance a wait is EXACTLY five?

zero.text: Not five and a bit. Exactly five... and the answer is zero. A single point has no width, so it holds no probability.

area.text: Probability lives on ranges, as area under the curve. Waits between two and eight minutes take up forty-seven percent of it.

cdf.text: In code, that's the area left of eight, minus the area left of two.

height-in.text: Which means the curve's height can't be a probability.

uniform.text: Spread a value evenly from zero to ten, and its curve is flat, a uniform, at a height of point one.

slice.text: Three to seven covers four tenths of the width, so it holds four tenths of the probability.

squeeze.text: Now squeeze all of it into half a unit. To keep the area at one, the height has to climb to two.

density.text: Two isn't a two hundred percent chance. It's a density, probability per unit of width. Only the area has to come to one.

quantile-in.text: Often, though, you need the question the other way round.

quantile.text: Say response times average two hundred milliseconds, and you want the time that ninety-five percent of requests beat.

across.text: Plot the share finished by each moment. Go across from ninety-five percent, then down... five hundred and ninety-nine milliseconds.

cutoff.text: That's a quantile, the area read backwards. It's how you set a cutoff, or a promise to customers.

normal-in.text: And of all these shapes, one turns up more than any other.
